title: How to Rehydrate After Drinking: Water vs ORS vs Sports Drinks
excerpt: The fastest way to rehydrate after drinking alcohol: why alcohol dehydrates you, how water, oral rehydration solutions, and sports drinks compare, a homemade ORS recipe, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: How to rehydrate after drinking: why water alone may fall short, ORS vs sports drinks vs water, a homemade rehydration recipe, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The answer first:** the best way to rehydrate after drinking is to sip an oral rehydration solution (ORS), or water with something salty to eat, a little at a time over a few hours. Plain water works fine after a light night. After a heavy night, or if you've been vomiting or have diarrhea, a drink with a bit of salt and a little sugar gets water into your body faster and keeps it there longer. Sports drinks sit in the middle. And whatever you choose, fixing your fluids will help, but it won't cure the whole hangover, because dehydration is only one part of why you feel bad.

If your question is simply whether drinking water helps a hangover at all, our guide to [whether water helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) answers that. This page is the practical plan: what to drink, how much, how fast, and when plain water isn't enough.

**The quick plan:**

- **Before bed:** a glass or two of water, or half a bottle of an ORS if you drank a lot.
- **When you wake up:** start sipping an ORS or water, about a cup every 15 to 20 minutes, not a liter in one go.
- **Eat something salty** as soon as your stomach allows: toast, crackers, broth, eggs, a banana with salted nuts.
- **Check your urine:** pale yellow means you're on track. Dark yellow or very little urine means keep going.
- **Skip the extra alcohol.** "Hair of the dog" just delays the problem.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most post-drinking dehydration is mild and fixes itself with fluids and food. Get medical help if you can't keep any fluids down for more than about 6 to 8 hours, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you've barely peed in 8 hours or more, you feel faint or confused, or your heart is racing and won't settle. **Call 911** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is having a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and the person should never be left to "sleep it off." Separately, if you usually drink heavily every day and you get shaking, sweating, anxiety or a racing heart when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, and it's worth talking to a doctor about. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Alcohol Dehydrates You in the First Place

Alcohol makes you pee more than you drink, and the reason is a hormone.

Your brain normally releases a hormone called **vasopressin** (also known as antidiuretic hormone, or ADH). Its job is to tell your kidneys to hold onto water instead of sending it to your bladder. Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, especially while your blood alcohol level is rising. With less of that "hold onto water" signal, your kidneys let more water go, and you make more urine than you otherwise would. That's why you end up breaking the seal and making repeated trips to the bathroom.

Several other things often pile on during a night out:

- **Vomiting and diarrhea.** Both drain water and salts (sodium, potassium, chloride) quickly. If either happened, you've lost electrolytes, not just water. Our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) covers that side of it.
- **Sweating.** Hot bars, dancing, and alcohol's tendency to widen blood vessels in the skin all add to sweat loss.
- **Not drinking anything else.** A night of beers or cocktails often replaces your usual water intake.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol fragments sleep, and you go many hours without drinking while you're out cold.

The result in the morning is the familiar set: thirst, dry mouth, dark urine, a headache, and feeling lightheaded when you stand up quickly.

## How Much Does Dehydration Actually Cause Your Hangover?

Less than most people assume. This matters, because it sets realistic expectations for what rehydrating will do.

Hangover researchers have looked at whether people who are more dehydrated have worse hangovers, and the link turns out to be weaker than the folk wisdom suggests. Hangover symptoms are driven by a mix of things: the inflammatory response to alcohol, the build-up of acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol), disrupted sleep, low blood sugar in some people, irritation of the stomach lining, and dehydration. Researchers in the field generally describe dehydration as a contributing factor rather than the main cause.

In practice that means:

- **Rehydrating reliably helps the dehydration-type symptoms:** thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and some of the headache.
- **It doesn't fix the rest:** the fatigue from poor sleep, the queasy stomach, the foggy head, and the general "poisoned" feeling usually take time.

So drink up, but don't be surprised if you feel noticeably better and still not great. If you want to understand the timeline, our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) walks through it.

## Water vs Oral Rehydration Solution vs Sports Drink

This is the core decision, so here's how the three main options compare.

| Drink | Sodium | Sugar | Best for | Downsides |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain water | None | None | Light drinking, sipping all day, alongside food | Leaves you peeing more of it out if you're low on salts |
| Oral rehydration solution (Pedialyte, pharmacy packets, homemade) | High | Low to moderate | Heavy nights, vomiting, diarrhea, feeling lightheaded | Salty taste, costs more than water |
| Sports drink (Gatorade, Powerade) | Low to moderate | High | Mild hangover when you want something that tastes good | Lots of sugar, not much sodium compared with an ORS |
| Coconut water | Low | Moderate | Potassium top-up, if you like it | Low in sodium, the main salt you lose |
| Electrolyte powders and tablets | Varies widely | Varies | Convenience, travel | Many are low in sodium; check the label |

### Why salt and sugar make water work better

Your small intestine has a built-in shortcut for absorbing water. A transporter in the gut lining moves sodium and glucose into your body together, and water follows them in. That's the principle behind oral rehydration therapy, which the World Health Organization calls one of the most important medical advances of the 20th century because it saved millions of lives from cholera and childhood diarrhea.

The trick is getting the balance right. A drink with some sodium and a modest amount of glucose is absorbed faster than plain water. A drink with too much sugar can do the opposite, because a very sugary liquid can actually pull water into the gut and slow things down. That's why a proper ORS is only mildly sweet, while soda and juice aren't good rehydration drinks.

### What the research on "most hydrating drinks" found

A frequently cited study from 2016 in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* (often called the Beverage Hydration Index study) compared how much of various drinks people still had in their bodies two hours later. An oral rehydration solution and milk were retained better than water, while sports drinks performed about the same as water. The volunteers were healthy and not hungover, so it doesn't directly test hangovers, but it supports the general idea: drinks with sodium (and in milk's case, protein and fat that slow emptying from the stomach) tend to stay in your body longer.

### Our honest ranking for a typical morning after

1. **Oral rehydration solution** if you drank heavily, vomited, had diarrhea, or feel dizzy when you stand.
2. **Water plus salty food** for most ordinary hangovers. This is cheap and works well.
3. **Sports drink plus a salty snack** if that's what you have or it's all your stomach will accept.
4. **Coconut water** as a pleasant extra, not the main event. Our [coconut water for hangovers](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) guide covers why its low sodium is the catch.

For a side-by-side look at specific products, see our [electrolyte drinks for hangovers comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) and the head-to-head on [Pedialyte vs Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover).

## What Is an Oral Rehydration Solution, and How Do You Use One?

An oral rehydration solution is a drink with a specific ratio of water, sodium, potassium, and glucose, designed to replace fluid and salts as efficiently as possible. The WHO's current formula is a "reduced osmolarity" version, meaning it's less concentrated than the original, which was found to work better and cause less stomach upset.

You can get an ORS in a few forms:

- **Ready-to-drink bottles** like Pedialyte and similar store brands.
- **Powder packets** you mix into water, sold in pharmacies (often near the diarrhea medicines) and as travel packs.
- **Homemade**, if you have nothing else (recipe below).

**How to drink it:** sip, don't gulp. A cup (about 250 ml) every 15 to 20 minutes is a reasonable pace for an adult. If you're nauseated, take even smaller sips, a mouthful every few minutes. Small, frequent amounts are much more likely to stay down than a big glass. Chilling it helps the taste.

**How much:** for a typical bad hangover, one to two liters of fluid spread over the morning, with at least some of it as an ORS, is a sensible target. You don't need to finish a set amount. Stop pushing when your urine is pale and you're no longer thirsty.

**Who should be careful:** people with kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure that's managed with a low-salt diet should check with their doctor before drinking a lot of high-sodium solutions.

### A simple homemade rehydration drink

If the stores are closed or you'd rather not buy anything, the classic WHO home recipe is:

- 1 liter of clean drinking water
- 6 level teaspoons of sugar
- ½ level teaspoon of salt

Stir until dissolved. Measure carefully. Too much salt is the main thing to avoid, and more sugar is not better. A squeeze of lemon or orange makes it more drinkable and adds a little potassium. Make a fresh batch each day.

If you'd rather not mix anything, a mug of salty broth or soup with a glass of water does a similar job and is easy on the stomach.

## How to Rehydrate Fast After Drinking: Step by Step

If you've just woken up feeling rough, this is the order that works best.

**1. Start with small sips.** Take a few mouthfuls of an ORS or water as soon as you're up. If your stomach is unsettled, wait a minute between sips. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more ways to settle it.

**2. Get some salt and carbs in.** Plain toast, crackers, pretzels, rice, a banana, or broth. Food supplies the sodium and potassium that make water stick, and it brings blood sugar back up. Eggs are a good next step once you can face real food; see [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover).

**3. Keep a steady pace.** Roughly a cup every 15 to 20 minutes for the first hour or two, then drink to thirst.

**4. Check your urine.** Within a few hours you should be peeing normally, and the color should move from dark yellow toward pale straw. That's your best home gauge.

**5. Add caffeine carefully, if you want it.** A normal cup of coffee or tea is fine for regular coffee drinkers and can ease a caffeine-withdrawal headache. Drink water alongside it.

**6. Rest.** Rehydration works whether or not you're on the couch, but sleep repairs the part of the hangover that fluids can't.

## How to Rehydrate Before Bed After Drinking

The best time to start rehydrating is before you sleep, because you're about to go seven or eight hours without drinking anything.

- **Drink one or two glasses of water** before you lie down. After a heavy night, a glass of ORS is better.
- **Leave a bottle by the bed** and sip if you wake up thirsty.
- **Have a small salty snack** if you can, like a few crackers or a slice of toast.
- **Don't force huge amounts.** Two liters at 2 a.m. mostly means you'll be up to pee and sleep even worse. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) covers the sleep side.

## Hydrating While You're Drinking (The Easiest Win)

Rehydrating the next morning is a cleanup job. Staying ahead of it is easier.

- **Alternate drinks with water.** A glass of water between each alcoholic drink slows your pace, which matters more than the water itself, and keeps you from falling further behind.
- **Eat a real meal beforehand.** Food slows how quickly alcohol hits your bloodstream and gives you a base of salts.
- **Watch the sugary mixers and shots.** They make it easy to drink faster.

For more on timing, see whether you should take [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking), and our broader guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## What Not to Drink When You're Trying to Rehydrate

- **More alcohol.** "Hair of the dog" puts off the hangover by topping up your blood alcohol, and it adds to the fluid loss. It's not a rehydration strategy, and if you find you need a drink in the morning to feel normal, that's worth talking to a doctor about.
- **Large amounts of soda or fruit juice.** The high sugar content can slow how quickly water gets absorbed and may worsen an upset stomach or diarrhea. A small glass of juice for blood sugar is fine.
- **Energy drinks.** High caffeine and sugar, and they can make a jittery, racing-heart morning worse. If your heart is pounding, see our guide on [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking).
- **Gallons of plain water, fast.** See the next section.

## Can You Drink Too Much Water After Drinking?

Yes, though it's uncommon. Drinking very large amounts of plain water in a short time can dilute the sodium in your blood, a condition called **hyponatremia**. Mild cases cause headache, nausea, and fatigue, which are easy to mistake for a worse hangover. Severe cases cause confusion, vomiting, and seizures and are a medical emergency.

The risk rises if you've lost a lot of salt (through vomiting, diarrhea, or heavy sweating) and replace it only with plain water, especially in large volumes. That's one more reason to include sodium from food or an ORS, sip rather than chug, and let thirst and urine color guide you. You don't need to hit a magic number.

## Do IV Drips Help You Rehydrate Faster?

IV hydration bars and mobile drip services advertise fast hangover relief. They do put fluid straight into your bloodstream. But for an ordinary hangover, there is no good evidence that an IV drip works better than drinking an ORS and eating, if you can keep fluids down. The vitamin "cocktails" in many drips also have little evidence behind them for hangovers. IVs carry small risks too, such as bruising, infection at the needle site, and vein irritation, and they're expensive.

Where an IV does make sense is in a medical setting, when someone can't keep any fluids down or is significantly dehydrated. If you're at that point, a doctor, urgent care, or the ER is the right place, because they can also check what else might be going on.

## How Long Does It Take to Rehydrate After Drinking?

For most people after a typical night out, steady sipping and a meal will correct the fluid loss within a few hours. A rough sign you're there: you've peed normally a couple of times and your urine is pale yellow.

It takes longer if you vomited repeatedly, had diarrhea, or drank very heavily, because you're replacing salts as well as water. It can also feel slower because the rest of the hangover (tiredness, poor sleep, stomach irritation) lingers after your fluids are back to normal. If your urine is still very dark or you've barely peed by late afternoon despite drinking, that's a reason to get checked.

## Signs You're Dehydrated vs Signs You Need Help

**Mild to moderate dehydration (manageable at home):**

- Thirst and dry mouth
- Dark yellow urine, or peeing less than usual
- Headache
- Feeling tired or lightheaded, especially when standing up

**Get medical help if you notice:**

- You can't keep fluids down for more than about 6 to 8 hours
- Little or no urine for 8 hours or more
- Confusion, extreme drowsiness, or fainting
- A racing heart that doesn't calm down with rest and fluids
- Vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
- Severe stomach pain

And again: anyone who has been drinking and can't be woken, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin needs emergency care now. Call 911. If you're worried about shaking, sweats, or anxiety after drinking, our [hangover shakes guide](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains the difference between ordinary hangover jitters and signs that need a doctor.

## Where DHM Fits (Honestly)

Rehydration deals with one part of a hangover. Some people also add a supplement aimed at a different part: how the body handles alcohol itself.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Animal research suggests it may help the body process alcohol and its by-products and reduce some of alcohol's effects on the brain. Human evidence is still limited, so there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright, and it is not a substitute for drinking less, eating, and rehydrating. It also doesn't rehydrate you; you still need fluids.

If you want to try it alongside the basics in this guide, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

To rehydrate after drinking, sip rather than chug, add salt, and go easy on sugar. Water with salty food handles most hangovers. An oral rehydration solution is the best option after a heavy night or if you've been vomiting or have diarrhea. Sports drinks are fine in a pinch, coconut water is a nice extra, and soda, energy drinks, and more alcohol don't help. Start with a glass or two before bed, watch your urine color the next day, and expect fluids to take the edge off rather than cure everything. And if you can't keep anything down or notice any of the warning signs above, get medical help rather than waiting it out.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the fastest way to rehydrate after drinking alcohol?**

Sip an oral rehydration solution (ORS) such as Pedialyte, a pharmacy rehydration packet, or a homemade salt-and-sugar mix, about a cup every 15 to 20 minutes, and eat something salty alongside it. The small amount of sugar and salt in an ORS helps your gut absorb water faster than plain water alone. If you only have water, drink it steadily with a salty snack rather than chugging a large amount at once.

**Is water enough to rehydrate after drinking?**

For a light night, yes. Water plus a normal meal replaces what you lost, because food supplies the sodium and potassium. Water alone works less well after a heavy night, vomiting, or diarrhea, because you've lost salts as well as fluid and plain water tends to be peed out faster. In those cases an oral rehydration solution or water with salty food is the better choice.

**Is Pedialyte or Gatorade better for rehydrating after alcohol?**

Pedialyte and other oral rehydration solutions are designed for rehydration, with more sodium and less sugar than a standard sports drink. Gatorade is designed for exercise and has more sugar and less sodium. Both are fine for a mild hangover. If you've been vomiting or have diarrhea, an ORS is the better match. A sports drink with a salty snack is a reasonable middle ground.

**How long does it take to rehydrate after drinking?**

Mild fluid loss usually corrects within a few hours of steady drinking and eating. You'll know you're getting there when you pee normally again and your urine turns pale yellow. Hangover symptoms often last longer than the dehydration itself, because dehydration is only one of several causes, so you may still feel rough after you're fully rehydrated.

**Should I drink water before bed after drinking alcohol?**

Yes, a glass or two of water before bed is a sensible habit, and an ORS is even better after a heavy night. Don't force down huge amounts, since you'll be up to pee all night and it won't help more. Keep a bottle by the bed and sip if you wake up thirsty.

**Does coffee dehydrate you more after drinking?**

A cup or two of coffee is unlikely to make your dehydration noticeably worse, especially if you drink coffee every day. Large amounts of caffeine have a mild diuretic effect, and coffee can upset an irritated stomach, so drink water or an ORS alongside it rather than instead of it.

**Do IV drips work better than drinking fluids for a hangover?**

For an ordinary hangover there is no good evidence that an IV drip helps more than drinking fluids and eating if you can keep them down. IVs make sense in a hospital when someone can't keep anything down or is seriously dehydrated. If you're vomiting so much that you can't hold down any liquids, that's a reason to see a doctor, not to book a drip bar.

**Can you drink too much water after drinking alcohol?**

Yes. Drinking very large amounts of plain water quickly can dilute the sodium in your blood, a condition called hyponatremia, which causes headache, nausea, and confusion that can look like a bad hangover. It's rare, but the safe approach is to sip steadily, include some salt from food or an ORS, and let thirst and urine color guide you.
